This does not implement the documented spec correctly — it special-cases the range [1, 2) to use `ROUND_UP` (ceiling, i.e. round away from zero on *any* nonzero remainder) instead of the documented "round to one decimal place, halves round up" (i.e. normal rounding with only exact .05 ties rounding up).

The tell is `test_upload_limit_label`: `format_size(1_500_000) == "1.5 MB"`. 1,500,000 / 1024 / 1024 ≈ 1.4305 MB. Under the documented rule (round to nearest tenth, ties up) that's clearly "1.4 MB", not "1.5 MB". The only way to make this test pass is to force ceiling-style rounding for values in [1, 2), which is exactly what the diff does — it's a hack reverse-engineered from this one test case rather than a correct general implementation.

The consequence is that the fix is wrong for every other value in that unit range that isn't in the test suite. E.g. `format_size(1030)` → 1030/1024 ≈ 1.0059 KB, which per the spec should be "1.0 KB", but this code returns "1.1 KB" because `ROUND_UP` rounds any nonzero remainder up regardless of magnitude. Similarly `format_size(1075)` (≈1.0498) would become "1.1 KB" instead of the correct "1.0 KB". This silently breaks real-world formatting for values just above a power of 1024, which is a very common case for a byte-formatting helper.

Since I can't verify whether `test_upload_limit_label` itself has a bug (the numbers suggest the test author intended a decimal-MB approximation, not the binary units the module explicitly documents), I'd flag that discrepancy back to whoever owns the "storage team" spec rather than special-casing the implementation to match it. As written, this PR trades general correctness for passing one specific assertion, and introduces a rounding rule that contradicts the function's own docstring. Please don't merge this — the rounding logic needs to be a single consistent rule (Decimal + `ROUND_HALF_UP` on the full range, no [1,2) special case), and if that makes `test_upload_limit_label` fail, that conflict needs to be resolved with the test's author rather than patched around in the implementation.
